claims.text: Post-processing heat or thermomechanical treatments induce subtle phase segregation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Post-processing heat or thermomechanical treatments induce nanoscale precipitation, particularly at grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation or precipitation reduces the alloy's ability to blunt or deflect propagating cracks.
Reduced crack blunting or deflection causes a loss of toughness under demanding loading conditions.
The initial alloy is an as-processed, compositionally homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
Annealing or ageing can promote nanoscale precipitates or compositional gradients relative to the as-processed state.
The relevant service loading includes elevated strain-rate or cyclic loading near or below ambient through moderate temperatures.
Precipitates or segregated phases form preferentially at grain boundaries.
Precipitates or segregated regions act as crack-initiation sites.
Precipitation or segregation impairs significant plastic deformation and reduces ductility.
Reduced ductility and impaired plastic deformation favor brittle failure over tough behavior.
Treated samples will have lower fracture toughness than identically tested as-processed samples.
Treated samples will initiate cracks earlier than identically tested as-processed samples.
Treated samples will shift toward brittle fracture behavior relative to the baseline.
The hypothesis applies where operational loading and thermal history can promote phase instability or precipitation.
